description: Solo entry from the Maldives. Building a Marswalk planner for Jezero Crater: a layered terrain map with route planning that helps astronauts plan safe, science-rich walks using NASA mission data.
summary: Marswalk Planner is a walkback-aware route planner for human EVAs at Jezero Crater, Mars. Apollo crews had to stay within walking distance of their lander in case the rover failed; on Mars, terrain slope decides how fast you can walk home. Place a habitat and pick science targets and the planner computes Fastest, Safest and Most science routes over real NASA terrain. It maps a safe-return zone, marks the turn-back point on each route and flags any route that breaks the EVA time or distance limit. It combines Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter elevation and imagery with Perseverance’s 45 km traverse and 12 sample sites, so a crew can see the trade-off between speed, safety and science before stepping outside.
details:
What it does
Marswalk Planner is a mission-planning map for a human walk (EVA) at Jezero Crater, Mars. The user places a habitat and adds science targets, and the planner builds a round trip: habitat → targets → habitat. It computes three alternative routes: Fastest, Safest and Most science. It compares them by walk time, distance, climb, maximum slope, metres of hazardous ground, sample sites passed and remaining EVA budget. Two safety limits apply to every plan: an EVA time budget and a maximum distance from the habitat. The map shades a safe-return zone (everywhere the astronaut can reach and still get home in time) and marks a turn-back point on any route that would break the budget. Layers can be switched on and off: CTX imagery, elevation, hillshade, slope, hazard classes, Perseverance’s 45 km traverse and 12 sample sites with science cards.

How it works

  1. Terrain: the MRO CTX elevation model and image mosaic are resampled onto one 20 m grid (equirectangular projection on the Mars sphere, radius 3,396,190 m). Slope and roughness are computed for every cell and each cell gets a hazard class: easy < 8°, moderate 8–15°, difficult 15–25°, no-go > 25°.
  2. Walking time: Tobler’s hiking function (slower uphill and on steep descents), scaled to 60% for a suited astronaut.
  3. Routing: an A* search finds the least-cost path. Cost is walking time multiplied by a hazard penalty that differs per route profile. The Most science route adds detours to nearby sample sites only while the walk stays within 90% of the time budget and the distance limit.
  4. Safety: a reverse Dijkstra search from the habitat gives the time to walk home from every cell. This produces the safe-return zone and the turn-back point.
  5. Rover data: the Perseverance traverse is shown as a line. Each sample is placed at the rover’s position on the sol its tube was sealed (approximate location).

Benefits and intended impact
EVA planning is a trade-off between speed, safety and science. Apollo crews had to stay within “walkback” range of their lander in case the rover failed and recent research (Olthoff, ICES 2018) argues walk-back limits should account for terrain slope. This tool makes that trade-off visible in seconds over real terrain: which route is quickest, which avoids steep ground, how much science a detour buys and where the crew must turn back. Possible uses include EVA traverse planning, astronaut training scenarios and public outreach about human exploration of Mars.

What makes it creative
Most Mars maps show layers. This one plans: it compares routes, applies safety limits and adds science stops only when they’re affordable. It also uses NASA’s real Perseverance route and sample sites as science targets, linking robotic exploration data directly to human EVA planning.

Factors considered

  • Mars coordinates: distances use the Mars radius, and the map scale bar is corrected for Mars.
  • Data limits: 20 m elevation data cannot see boulders smaller than about 20 m, so slope near cliffs is underestimated.
  • Assumptions: hazard thresholds and suit speed are design assumptions, stated in the app, not NASA requirements.
  • Performance: routing runs in the browser in about half a second, so plans update immediately when targets or limits change.
  • This is an educational prototype, not for operational use.

Tools
Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) for terrain preprocessing; JavaScript and Leaflet for the web app; GitHub Pages for hosting.
Live app: https://zeykahmed.github.io/marswalk-planner/
Code: https://github.com/zeykahmed/marswalk-planner

Use of AI and my role
I used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to write the code (Python preprocessing and the JavaScript web app) and to help draft the slides and this text. I directed and evaluated the work: I chose the challenge and kept the scope on mission planning rather than map layers; tested the app and checked that routes and hazards made sense on the terrain; pushed for a more distinctive framing, which led to the walkback-limit focus; removed claims that weren’t accurate; and deployed and debugged the live site on GitHub Pages. All maps and screenshots are rendered by the app’s code from NASA data; no images were created with an image-generation model, so no AI watermarks are needed.

I approached this hackathon as a learning project: I’m moving into geospatial science, and working through a real terrain-analysis and routing workflow on NASA data (from raw elevation models to slope, cost surfaces and least-cost paths) was a way to understand how these pipelines fit together in practice.
